title: How a Healthy Church Board or Elder Team Works
subtitle: A practical guide to church governance, biblical plurality, and the kind of trust that lets a board or elder team lead together without splitting or stalling.

sections.title: God Never Built a Church Around One Man
sections.body:
Read the New Testament looking for the solo leader and you will not find him. Paul appointed elders, plural, in every church. The church at Antioch had prophets and teachers, a list of names, not a name. The Jerusalem council was a room of leaders reasoning together, not a single voice handing down a verdict. The pattern is everywhere, and it is consistent, and most churches have quietly abandoned it.

Plurality is not committee culture imported into the church. It is a confession about human nature. One man, however gifted, however godly, has blind spots he cannot see by definition, because that is what a blind spot is. He needs other men beside him who can see what he cannot, who can tell him no, who can carry what he cannot carry alone. The board or the elder team exists because no single sinner should hold unchecked authority over the people of God.

Not a chairman with advisors. A body. The healthy elder team is not a leader surrounded by people who ratify him. It is a group of qualified men who share the weight, share the authority, and share the account they will give. The moment one man can do whatever he wants and the rest exist to approve it, you do not have an elder team. You have a platform with a quorum.

sections.title: The Board Is Only as Healthy as Its Members
sections.body:
A church will not rise above its leaders, and its leaders will not rise above their character. So the first question about any board is not how it functions but who is on it, and most boards are dysfunctional because of who was let in.

The qualifications in First Timothy and Titus are almost entirely about character, not competence. Above reproach. Faithful to his wife. Not quarrelsome. Not a lover of money. Manages his own household well. There is exactly one skill on the list, able to teach, and the rest is who the man is when no one is watching. We invert this constantly. We put the successful businessman on the board because he understands budgets, never asking whether he is gentle, never asking whether he is humble, and then we are mystified when board meetings turn into hostile takeovers.

Choose elders for their character or repent of it later. The wealthy donor who bullies, the gifted leader who cannot be told no, the loyal friend who has no spine, every one of them will cost the church more than they ever gave. Slow down the process. Watch a man for years before you lay hands on him. A board of qualified men can survive almost anything. A board of unqualified men cannot survive itself.

sections.title: Without Trust You Have a Standoff
sections.body:
A board can have the right structure, the right members, the right bylaws, and still be dead, because the thing that makes a board actually work is not on the org chart. It is trust, and trust is built in private long before it is tested in public.

Trust is the willingness to assume the best about the brother across the table. It means I can disagree with you sharply about the building project and still believe you love this church as much as I do. Where trust is present, conflict is productive, because we are fighting about the issue. Where trust is absent, every disagreement becomes an accusation, every motion becomes a maneuver, and the board splits into factions that meet in parking lots after the meeting to plan the next one.

You cannot legislate trust. You build it. You eat together before you vote together. You pray for one another by name. You watch one another keep small promises until you are willing to risk a large one. The boards that fracture are almost never undone by a single issue. They are undone by years of relational neglect that left them with no reservoir to draw on when the hard issue finally came. Build the relationships in peacetime, because you will spend them in war.

sections.title: How a Healthy Board Actually Decides
sections.body:
A board exists to decide, and a board that cannot decide is not a board, it is a discussion group with a treasurer. But the way a board decides matters as much as what it decides, and the healthy ones share a few habits the dysfunctional ones never learned.

They aim for unity, not just a majority. A five to four vote on a major direction is a wound waiting to open, so a healthy board keeps talking, keeps praying, keeps listening until the dissenters are either persuaded or genuinely at peace with being overruled. They distinguish the few decisions that belong to them from the many that belong to the staff, so they are not relitigating the color of the carpet while the mission drifts. And they keep confidence absolutely, because a board member who reports the room to his friends has murdered the trust that made the room work.

When the decision is made, they own it together. The elder who voted against the new direction defends it in the hallway as if it were his own, because the body decided and he is part of the body. That is the test of a real board. Not whether they agree, but whether they can disagree, decide, and then stand together as though they had agreed all along.

sections.title: You Will Give an Account for Souls
sections.body:
Hebrews says something to those who lead that should sober every man who has ever sat on a church board. They keep watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account. Not an account for the budget. Not an account for the building. An account for souls.

We forget this. We turn the board into a business meeting, treat the church like a corporation with a Jesus theme, and argue about money and policy as though that were the work. It is not the work. The work is the eternal welfare of the people who walked in on Sunday morning trusting that the men leading them were watching over them before God. Every decision that board makes lands on a real soul somewhere, and the men who made it will answer for it.

I have sat in those rooms and felt the weight lift and turn into mere management, and I have let it, because management is easier than shepherding. The healthy board never forgets what it is holding. These are not stakeholders. They are sheep, bought with blood, and the men around the table are undershepherds who will look the Chief Shepherd in the eye and explain how they led his flock. Lead like that day is coming. It is.
